I am 63 years old, I never went to school, and I have worked this land in Quzhou for 30 years. I know every mu of my 14 mu farm by feel, not by books. My household is just me and my husband now—our children have left—so our backs are the only backs we have. We cannot break them.

It is early spring. My winter wheat is already in the field, sown last October with improved seed I saved from the year before. This year I will manage 10 mu for wheat and maize together, and 4 mu for cotton. Ten mu in the wheat-maize rotation gives us grain to eat and sell, and it is easier on the body because the machines help with harvest and planting. Cotton pays more per jin, but it is a devil for labor—spraying, pruning, and picking all by hand. At our age, 4 mu of cotton is enough. Any more and we would not sleep.

For the wheat that is already green, I will topdress it with urea when the weather warms and irrigate it four times from our well, especially at heading and grain-filling when the crop is thirsty. I will spray three times for disease and pests. After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize seed directly into the stubble with no tillage. This saves diesel, time, and my husband's strength. The maize will need two irrigations and two sprayings, and it will come off in October.

For cotton, I will rotary-till the 4 mu plot and apply basal compound fertilizer, then sow improved cotton seed in late April. Cotton must be watered three times and sprayed twelve times through the season to fight bollworm and aphids, but I have done this for decades and I know the rhythm. I expect about 500 jin per mu from the cotton, and about 1000 jin per mu from both the wheat and the maize.

This is my plan. It is the same plan I have trusted for years—enough grain to be safe, enough cotton for cash, and not so much that two old farmers collapse.
